## Introduction

In this workflow, we tackle a common geospatial problem: extracting data from stylized news graphics (like election heatmaps) and converting them into GIS-ready formats.

Rather than just cleaning the rough edges of a scraped SVG, we will use a **reconstruction technique**. We will:

1. **Scrape** the electoral map to get rough constituency shapes (@sec-scrape, @sec-parse).
2. **Georeference** the shapes to align them with real coordinates (@sec-georef).
3. **Reconstruct** the precise boundaries by grouping official administrative "Wards" based on which constituency shape they fall into (@sec-wards).

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-workflow
%%| fig-cap: "The workflow: rough shapes from the scraped map, precise boundaries from the wards."
flowchart LR
  A["Scrape<br/>SVG"] --> B["Parse and<br/>georeference"]
  B --> C["Rough<br/>shapes"]
  W["Official<br/>wards"] --> D["Match each ward<br/>to a shape"]
  C --> D
  D --> E["Dissolve by<br/>constituency"]
  E --> F["Final<br/>GeoJSON"]
```
:::

::: {.column-margin}
The constituency map comes from the [2079 general election heatmap](https://generalelection2079.ekantipur.com/heatmap) on ekantipur. Ward boundaries are the official administrative layer saved in this post's `data/` folder.
:::

## Setup and Libraries

We use `sf` for spatial operations and `rvest` for scraping. We also define paths for our inputs (official ward data) and outputs.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the setup code"

library(sf)       # Spatial data handling
library(xml2)     # Parsing XML/SVG
library(rvest)    # Web scraping
library(httr2)    # HTTP requests
library(stringr)  # String manipulation
library(dplyr)    # Data manipulation
library(here)     # Robust project-relative paths

post_dir <- here("posts", "nepal-election-geojson") # <1>

wards_geojson_path    <- here::here(post_dir, "data", "nepal-wards.gpkg") # <2>
national_geojson_path <- here::here(post_dir, "data", "nepal-national.gpkg")

output_svg_path       <- here::here(post_dir, "output", "nepal_electoral_map.svg") # <3>
rough_map_path <- here::here(post_dir, "output", "nepal_svg_rough.geojson")
output_geojson_path   <- here::here(post_dir, "output", "nepal_electoral_map.geojson")

if (!dir.exists(dirname(output_svg_path))) dir.create(dirname(output_svg_path), recursive = TRUE) # <4>
```

1. The path to this post's own folder, so the code runs from anywhere in the project.
2. Official ward and national boundaries, used as the reference.
3. Where the three outputs are written.
4. Create the output folder if it is missing.

## Scraping the SVG {#sec-scrape}

We use `httr2` to fetch the webpage and `rvest` to extract the specific SVG element containing the map. We also inject some CSS to ensure the map renders correctly if viewed in a browser (e.g., setting the viewBox and handling overflow).

```{r}
#| label: scrape-svg

url <- "https://generalelection2079.ekantipur.com/heatmap"

message("Fetching data from: ", url)

tryCatch({
  req <- request(url) |>
    req_user_agent("Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36") # <1>

  resp <- req_perform(req)
  html_content <- resp_body_html(resp)

  svg_node <- html_element(html_content, xpath = "//svg[.//pattern[@id='np__BG']]") # <2>

  if (!inherits(svg_node, "xml_missing")) {
    xml_set_attr(svg_node, "viewBox", "0 0 1920 1080") # <3>

    css_styles <- "
      path { fill: #cccccc; stroke: #fff; cursor: pointer; stroke-width: 1.75px; }
      path:hover { opacity: 0.9; }
      .national-park { fill: #55e5a5 !important; }
      svg { overflow: visible !important; }
    "
    xml_add_child(svg_node, "style", css_styles, .where = 0) # <4>

    write_xml(svg_node, output_svg_path)
    message("Success! Raw SVG saved to: ", output_svg_path)

  } else {
    warning("SVG element not found on the page.")
  }
}, error = function(e) {
  message("Error fetching URL: ", e$message)
})

if (!exists("svg_node") && file.exists(output_svg_path)) { # <5>
  message("Using the previously saved SVG: ", output_svg_path)
  svg_node <- read_xml(output_svg_path)
}
```

1. Send a browser-like user agent, because the site can refuse bare requests.
2. Pick the one `<svg>` that carries this map's background pattern.
3. Fix the viewBox at 1920 by 1080 so every run uses the same coordinate system.
4. Inject CSS so the saved SVG also looks right when opened in a browser.
5. The source site is sometimes down: fall back to the SVG saved by an earlier run.

## Parsing SVG Paths to Geometry {#sec-parse}

SVG paths are stored as strings in the `d` attribute. We need a robust parser to convert these strings into numerical coordinates. This function handles messy spacing and implicit commands often found in web SVGs.

```{r}
#| label: parse-geometry
#| lst-label: lst-parse
#| lst-cap: "Turning an SVG path string into polygon coordinates"

parse_d_robust <- function(d) {
  d_clean <- str_replace_all(d, "-", " -") # <1>
  d_clean <- str_replace_all(d_clean, "[a-zA-Z]", " ") # <2>
  nums <- as.numeric(str_split(d_clean, "[\\s,]+")[[1]])
  nums <- nums[!is.na(nums)]

  if(length(nums) < 4) return(NULL)

  mtx <- matrix(nums, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE) # <3>
  if (!all(mtx[1,] == mtx[nrow(mtx),])) mtx <- rbind(mtx, mtx[1,]) # <4>
  if (nrow(mtx) < 4) return(NULL)

  return(mtx)
}

path_nodes <- xml_find_all(svg_node, "//*[local-name()='path']")

polys_list <- list()
id_list <- character()

for (i in seq_along(path_nodes)) {
  d_attr <- xml_attr(path_nodes[i], "d")
  id_val <- xml_attr(path_nodes[i], "data-slug")

  if (is.na(id_val) || id_val == "") next # <5>

  coords <- parse_d_robust(d_attr)
  if (!is.null(coords)) {
    polys_list[[length(polys_list) + 1]] <- st_polygon(list(coords))
    id_list <- c(id_list, id_val)
  }
}

if (length(polys_list) == 0) stop("No valid map districts found after filtering.")

nepal_sf <- st_sf(constituency_id = id_list, geometry = st_sfc(polys_list)) # <6>
```

1. Minified paths write negative numbers without a separator (`100-100`), so put a space before each minus sign.
2. Remove the path commands (`M`, `L`, `C` and so on) and keep only the numbers.
3. Pair the numbers up as x and y coordinates.
4. Close the ring if the path is open; a polygon must end where it starts.
5. Skip paths with no `data-slug`: they are buttons and background rectangles, not constituencies.
6. The result is still in raw SVG coordinates, which is why the next step georeferences it.

The parser in @lst-parse is deliberately forgiving, because the paths come straight from a web page.

## Georeferencing (Affine Transformation) {#sec-georef}

The extracted SVG uses screen coordinates (pixels). To make this map useful, we must align it with the real world (Longitude/Latitude).

We do this by calculating the bounding box of a reference map (`data/nepal-national.geojson`) and scaling our SVG to fit those dimensions.

```{r}
#| label: transform-geometry

if (!file.exists(national_geojson_path)) stop("Reference map not found.")

nepal_ref <- st_read(national_geojson_path, quiet = TRUE)

target_bbox <- st_bbox(st_transform(nepal_ref, 3857)) # <1>

flip_matrix <- matrix(c(1, 0, 0, -1), ncol = 2)
nepal_sf$geometry <- nepal_sf$geometry * flip_matrix # <2>

# Calculate Scale Factors
src_bbox <- st_bbox(nepal_sf)
src_w <- src_bbox$xmax - src_bbox$xmin
src_h <- src_bbox$ymax - src_bbox$ymin

tgt_w <- target_bbox$xmax - target_bbox$xmin
tgt_h <- target_bbox$ymax - target_bbox$ymin

nepal_sf$geometry <- nepal_sf$geometry - c(src_bbox$xmin, src_bbox$ymin) # <3>

scale_matrix <- matrix(c(tgt_w / src_w, 0, 0, tgt_h / src_h), ncol = 2)
nepal_sf$geometry <- nepal_sf$geometry * scale_matrix # <4>

nepal_sf$geometry <- nepal_sf$geometry + c(target_bbox$xmin, target_bbox$ymin) # <5>

st_crs(nepal_sf) <- 3857 # <6>
```

1. The reference map, projected to Web Mercator (EPSG:3857), gives the target size and aspect ratio for a web map.
2. Flip the y-axis: SVG puts the origin at the top left, maps put it at the bottom left.
3. Shift the SVG so its lower-left corner sits at (0, 0).
4. Stretch it to the same width and height as the reference map.
5. Shift it onto the reference map's position.
6. Declare the coordinate system, now that the numbers really are Web Mercator metres.

```{r eval = knitr::is_html_output()}
# Create interactive map
mapview::mapview(nepal_sf, map.types = "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas")
```

```{r}
#| label: export-scraped-svg

# Save the georeferenced SVG map before the ward dissolve
# We use 'delete_dsn = TRUE' to overwrite any old versions
st_write(
    nepal_sf,
    rough_map_path,
    driver = "GeoJSON",
    delete_dsn = TRUE,
    quiet = TRUE
)

message("Rough SVG map saved to: ", rough_map_path)
```

## Reconstruction via Wards {#sec-wards}

The transformed SVG is roughly accurate but has "jagged" borders and low-quality topology. To fix this, we use the **Wards** method:

1.  Convert high-quality Ward polygons to centroids.
2.  Check which rough SVG shape each Ward centroid falls into.
3.  Dissolve (merge) the Ward polygons based on that grouping.

This results in a map that perfectly matches official administrative boundaries.

```{r}
#| label: reconstruction-wards

message("Reconstructing boundaries using Wards...")

if (!file.exists(wards_geojson_path)) stop("Wards GeoJSON not found.")
wards <- st_read(wards_geojson_path, quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_make_valid()

wards_utm <- st_transform(wards, 32645) # <1>
nepal_utm <- st_transform(nepal_sf, 32645) |> st_make_valid()

message("Matching wards to constituencies...")
sf_use_s2(FALSE) # <2>
ward_centroids <- st_centroid(wards_utm)
nearest_indices <- st_nearest_feature(ward_centroids, nepal_utm) # <3>
wards_utm$constituency_id <- nepal_utm$constituency_id[nearest_indices]

message("Dissolving geometries and removing slivers...")

final_map_utm <- wards_utm |>
  group_by(constituency_id) |>
  summarise(geometry = st_union(geom)) |> # <4>
  st_make_valid() |>
  st_buffer(dist = 1) |> # <5>
  st_buffer(dist = -1) |>
  st_make_valid()

final_map <- st_transform(final_map_utm, 4326) # <6>
```

1. Work in metres: Nepal falls mostly in UTM zone 45N (EPSG:32645), which keeps the cleanup accurate.
2. Use the planar GEOS engine rather than spherical S2 for these joins.
3. Each ward centroid is matched to the nearest rough constituency shape.
4. Merge the wards that share a constituency into one polygon.
5. Remove slivers by growing the shapes 1 metre and shrinking them back.
6. Back to WGS84 (longitude and latitude) for the GeoJSON export.

```{r eval = knitr::is_html_output()}
# Create interactive map. The widget embeds every vertex in the page, so map a
# simplified copy (200 m tolerance). The exported GeoJSON below stays full resolution.
final_map_preview <- final_map_utm |>
  sf::st_simplify(preserveTopology = TRUE, dTolerance = 200) |>
  st_transform(4326)

mapview::mapview(final_map_preview, map.types = "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas")
```

```{r}
# 6. Save Result
st_write(
    final_map,
    output_geojson_path,
    driver = "GeoJSON",
    layer_options = "COORDINATE_PRECISION=6",
    delete_dsn = TRUE,
    quiet = TRUE
)

message("Reconstruction Complete! Saved to: ", output_geojson_path)
```
